passages.t: ‘The venom of vipers is on their lips’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The prayer is for rescue from violent men. “Rescue me, O LORD, from evil men. Protect me from men of violence” (verse 1). They plan evil and stir up fights “all day long” (verse 2). “They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips” (verse 3). They set hidden traps along his path (verse 5).

The singer holds on to God. “I say to the LORD, ‘You are my God’” (verse 6). “O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, You shield my head in the day of battle” (verse 7).

Then he asks God to turn the enemies' own trouble back on them. “May burning coals fall on them; may they be thrown into the fire, into the miry pits, never to rise again” (verse 10). “May no slanderer be established in the land” (verse 11).

He ends with what he knows. “I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy” (verse 12). “Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Psalms 140 to 143 are four prayers in a row from someone under attack. The enemies here fight with words as much as weapons: lies, slander and plots. A snake's bite is quick and its poison works unseen, which is why the singer compares lying tongues to vipers.

The traps of verse 5 come from hunting: a snare, a net, a lure set along a path where an animal will walk. The singer feels hunted.

‘You shield my head in the day of battle’ is the picture of a helmet. God himself is his protection.

Notice who the singer stands with in verse 12: the poor and the needy. The violent men are the kind who prey on the weak. His prayer is for justice, not only for himself.

‘Selah’ comes three times in this psalm (verses 3, 5 and 8). The book page explains that no one is sure what it means.
passages.later:
Paul gathers lines from the Psalms to show that all people are under sin, and he includes verse 3: “The venom of vipers is on their lips” (Romans 3:13).

Burning coals also appear in Proverbs, but in a surprising way: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (Proverbs 25:21), it says, “For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head” (Proverbs 25:22). Paul quotes it in Romans 12:20. There the coals come from kindness.
passages.hard: Verses 9 to 11 ask God to bring the enemies' own evil down on them. Like the other cursing psalms, this prayer hands the matter to God; the singer does not plan to act himself. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read such lines. No reading of them makes it right to harm anyone.
passages.asks:
Have you been hurt by someone's words: slander, gossip, a lie that spread? Psalm 140 knows that words can poison. It takes that hurt to God.

And verse 12 asks you to stand where the singer stands: with the poor and needy, trusting that God sees what is done to them. Do your own words heal or harm?
